title: CHAPTER FIVE. On the nature of God in general; what God is
latin: CAPUT QUINTUM, De natura Dei in genere. Atque ita ostendimus, unum esse Deum: nunc videbimus, quaenam sit illius natura, & qualem se nobis qua operibus, qua verbo revelaverit. Hujus enim notitia nobis oppido est necessaria, tum quia verum Deum omniaque fictitia numina discriminat, tum quia ad eum timendum, amandum, honorandum, fiduciamque in ipsum collocandam, nos excitat. Quid igitur Deus est? I. Deus est ens simpliciter, summum, vivens integre atque independens. Ex iis, quae cap. 3. docuimus, manifestum quidem est, Dei essentiam definitione explicari non posse, quod & ex hoc principio evidenter concluditur, nempe quod quaecunque definiuntur proprie, genere constant ac differentia. Atqui Deus nullum genus supra se habet, quia omnia genera transcendit, neque veram differentiam capit, quia haec sine genere, quod contrahat ac determinet, nusquam reperitur, id quod in attributo infinitatis plenius demonstrabitur atque inter gentiles a Platone recte assertum fuit. Describi tamen potest aliqua ratione per attributa quaedam, quae naturae divinae excellentiam declarant, ac sunt velut notae, quibus Deus ab aliis rebus omnibus distinguitur.
english: CHAPTER FIVE. On the nature of God in general.

And so we have shown that God is one: now we will see what His nature is, and of what sort He has revealed Himself to us both by works and by the Word. For knowledge of this is exceedingly necessary for us, both because it discriminates the true God from all fictitious divinities, and because it stirs us to fear, love, and honor Him, and to place our trust in Him.

What then is God? I. God is being simply, the highest, living integrally and independently. From what we taught in chapter 3 it is plain that God's essence cannot be explained by a definition, which is also clearly concluded from this principle: whatever things are properly defined consist of genus and difference. But God has no genus above Himself, because He transcends all genera, nor does He admit a true difference, because that is nowhere found without a genus which contracts and determines it — which will be more fully demonstrated in the attribute of infinity, and was rightly asserted among the Gentiles by Plato. Yet He can be described in some measure by certain attributes which declare the excellence of the divine nature and are as it were marks by which God is distinguished from all other things.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): CHAPTER FIVE. Concerning ye nature belonging toward God in general. And so we have shown that God is one: now we will see what His nature is, plus of what sort He has revealed Himself unto us both by works plus by ye Word. For knowledge belonging toward this stands exceedingly necessary for us, both because it discriminates ye true God from all fictitious divinities, plus because unto fearing, loving, honoring Him, plus placing trust in Him, it stirs us. What then is God? I. God is being simply, ye highest, living integrally plus independently. From those things which in chapter 3 we taught it is plain that God's essence by a definition cannot be explained, which also from this principle is clearly concluded: whatever things properly are defined consist of genus plus difference. But God no genus above Himself has, because all genera He transcends, nor a true difference does He admit, because that without a genus which contracts plus determines is nowhere found — which in ye attribute belonging toward infinity more fully will be demonstrated, plus among ye Gentiles by Plato was rightly asserted. Yet by certain attributes which ye excellence belonging toward ye divine nature declare He can in some measure be described, plus they stand as marks by which God from all other things is distinguished.

title: Common and proper ratio of divine perfection; description by negation and degrees
latin: Est autem ratio communis, quam in Deo concipimus, esse illud absolutum, quod quasi gradum quendam communem in omni ente cogitare solemus. Ratio autem propria est perfectio quaedam propria, quem partim comparatione ad conceptum nostrum declarare possumus, quod secundum naturam suam tantum concipiatur positive, partim per comparationem ad oppositum, quod excludat omnem imperfectionem creaturae; qua quodammodo est non ens: idque innuimus, cum Deum infinitum dicimus, cap. 9. Atque ita explicamus perfectionem Dei per negationem rationis. Nam imperfectionem sive non ens negare, est in rei veritate affirmatio, sed quae concipitur in modum negationis ob fictionem praecedentem, qua non ens instar entis concipitur. Ut autem gradus essendi Deo proprius aliquo modo intelligatur, considerandae sunt omnes quasi partes seu gradus perfectionis, quos in rebus creatis ullo modo distributos videmus: quibus in unum collectis haec omnia, quae in creaturis divisa sunt, in Deo simplicissime & infinites etiam plura esse cogitabimus multo magis, quam omnes gradus luminis in reliquis corporibus parcius apparentes, in sole simul eminenter ac perfectiore quodammodo esse dicimus. Tales descriptiones frequentes sunt cum in divinis literis, tum apud ecclesiasticos & profanos autores. Nos hanc in praesentiarum eligimus, tum quia Deum ab aliis rebus omnibus sufficienter distinguit, tum quia principium quoddam nobis largitur, quod sit tanquam fundamentum, cui reliqua omnia Dei attributa superstruantur.
english: But the common ratio which we conceive in God is that absolute which we are accustomed to think of as a certain common grade in every being. The proper ratio, however, is a certain proper perfection, which we can declare partly by comparison to our concept — that according to His nature it is conceived only positively — partly by comparison to the opposite, which excludes every imperfection of the creature, by which the creature is in a manner non-being: and that we intimate when we call God infinite (chapter 9).

And so we explain God's perfection by negation of a ratio. For to deny imperfection or non-being is in the truth of the thing an affirmation, but one conceived in the manner of a negation because of a preceding fiction by which non-being is conceived after the likeness of being. And that God's own grade of being may somehow be understood, all the quasi-parts or grades of perfection which we see distributed in any way in created things are to be considered: these gathered into one, we will think that all which are divided in creatures are in God most simply and infinitely even more — much more than we say all the grades of light that appear more sparsely in other bodies are at once eminently and in a more perfect manner in the sun.

Such descriptions are frequent both in the divine letters and among ecclesiastical and pagan authors. We choose this one for the present, both because it sufficiently distinguishes God from all other things, and because it grants us a certain principle that is as it were a foundation on which all the remaining attributes of God may be built.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): But ye common ratio which in God we conceive is that absolute which as a certain common grade in every being we are accustomed to think. Ye proper ratio however stands as a certain proper perfection, which partly by comparison unto our concept we can declare — that according to His nature only positively it is conceived — partly by comparison unto ye opposite, which every imperfection belonging toward ye creature excludes, by which ye creature in a manner is non-being: plus that we intimate when God infinite we call (chapter 9). And so God's perfection by negation belonging toward a ratio we explain. For to deny imperfection or non-being stands in ye truth belonging toward ye thing as an affirmation, but one conceived in ye manner belonging toward a negation because of a preceding fiction by which non-being after ye likeness belonging toward being is conceived. And that God's own grade belonging toward being somehow may be understood, all ye quasi-parts or grades belonging toward perfection which in created things in any way distributed we see are to be considered: these into one gathered, we will think that all which in creatures are divided in God most simply plus infinitely even more are — much more than all ye grades belonging toward light more sparsely in other bodies appearing at once eminently plus in a more perfect manner in ye sun we say are. Such descriptions both in ye divine letters plus among ecclesiastical plus pagan authors are frequent. This one for ye present we choose, both because God from all other things sufficiently it distinguishes, plus because a certain principle unto us it grants that as a foundation stands on which all ye remaining attributes belonging toward God may be built.

title: PRINCIPIO: ens said of God; Exodus 3:14; analogical not univocal predication
latin: PRINCIPIO, Ens hic loco generis ponitur, recteque dicitur de Deo. Nam Deus perfectissimo modo est, quia a seipso exsistit, ut cap. 2. ostendimus. Atque hinc sibimetipsi ab eo, quod est esse, nomen imposuit, Exod. 3.14. quo declarat, se esse ENS SIMPLICITER, a quo, per quem & in quem sunt omnia. Ita enim se ab aliis discernit ut sese esse dicat simpliciter, cetera vero quodammodo non esse significet, Esai. 40.15.17; Psal. 62.10. Neque tamen eodem modo de Deo, ut de creaturis, ens omnino dicitur. Nam ratio entis in Deo infinite excedit eam, quae est in creaturis: unde non univoce, sed analogice de Deo & creaturis ens praedicatur: quum haec non dicantur entia, nisi per attributionem ad illum, a quo habent, ut entia sint & dicantur. Deus igitur maxime proprie & substantialiter est ens. Neque unitatem destruimus, cum dicimus, Deus est ens. Copula enim hic non copulat diversa: neque plura secundum rem, sed secundum rationes formales a nobis conceptas & semper sumitur in divinis propositionibus essentialiter. Deus ipse revelavit Mosi hoc esse nomen suum: Ego sum, qui sum. postea vero dixit, DOMINUS Deus tuus, Deus unus est. Quapropter statuendum est, de Deo nihil dici essentialius.
english: IN THE FIRST PLACE, Being is here put in the place of a genus, and is rightly said of God. For God is in the most perfect manner, because He exists from Himself, as we showed in chapter 2. And hence He imposed on Himself a name from that which is to be (Exodus 3:14), by which He declares that He is BEING SIMPLY, from whom, through whom, and in whom are all things. For so He discerns Himself from others that He says Himself to be simply, but signifies that the rest in a manner are not (Isaiah 40:15, 17; Psalm 62:10).

Yet Being is not said of God altogether in the same way as of creatures. For the ratio of being in God infinitely exceeds that which is in creatures: from which Being is predicated of God and creatures not univocally but analogically — since these are not called beings except by attribution to Him from whom they have it that they are and are called beings. God therefore most properly and substantially is being. Nor do we destroy unity when we say God is being. For the copula here does not couple diverse things, nor several according to the thing, but according to formal rationes conceived by us, and in divine propositions is always taken essentially.
God Himself revealed to Moses that this is His name: I am who I am. Afterwards He said, the LORD your God, God is one. Therefore it is to be established that nothing is said of God more essentially.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): IN YE FIRST PLACE, Being here in ye place belonging toward a genus is put, plus rightly of God is said. For God in ye most perfect manner is, because from Himself He exists, as in chapter 2 we showed. And hence upon Himself a name from that which is to be He imposed (Exodus 3:14), by which He declares that He is BEING SIMPLY, from whom, through whom plus in whom all things are. For so Himself from others He discerns that Himself to be simply He says, but that ye rest in a manner are not He signifies (Isaiah 40:15, 17; Psalm 62:10). Yet Being is not of God altogether in ye same way as of creatures said. For ye ratio belonging toward being in God infinitely exceeds that which in creatures is: from which Being of God plus creatures not univocally but analogically is predicated — since these are not called beings except by attribution unto Him from whom they have it that they are plus are called beings. God therefore most properly plus substantially is being. Nor unity do we destroy when God is being we say. For ye copula here does not couple diverse things, nor several according to ye thing, but according to formal rationes by us conceived, plus in divine propositions always essentially is taken. God Himself unto Moses revealed that this is His name: I am who I am. Afterwards He said, ye LORD your God, God is one. Therefore it is to be established that nothing of God more essentially is said.

title: Why ens is most essential: four reasons; Bernard and Augustine on divine identity
latin: Id quod varie constat. 1. Deus non est in genere, sed excedit omnia. Ens vero praescindit omnem modum exsistendi genericum & relinquit significatum in sua amplitudine infinita. Non enim potest finiri ens, sed hoc & illud ens. Ens supergreditur tempora, loca & modos in iis exsistendi. 2. Hoc vocabulum efficit ut mens nostra vagetur ad infinitum pelagus essentiae divinae, ita ut non inveniamus ubi sistamus intuitum. Qui autem putat se ultra ens aliud invenire, is entis rationem nondum habuit. 3. Ens dicit praesens aeternitatis, auferens futurum & praeteritum. Ista enim non sunt in Deo, sed in rebus patientibus successionem. Successio autem ex mutabilitate est. Idcirco indicat etiam aeternitatem & immutabilitatem. Nulla autem creatura potest hoc nomine exquisite nominari, quatenus nomen est, sed quatenus participium. Participant enim aliquam entitatem, non tamen sunt entia, sed aliqua entia. Sic homo non est ens, sed aliquod ens. Et quamvis praedicetur sine additione ens de cunctis, tamen semper intelligitur cum additione & contractione, de Deo autem absolute. Et haec est differentia inter ens praedicabile & ens primum, ut est apud Thomam Aquinatem in libello de ente & essentia. Deus enim est omnia eminenter. Quapropter ejus nomen est omne nomen, ut dixit Trismegistus. 4. In omni re invenitur accidens excepto Deo. Accidens autem differt a substantia rei. Quapropter nequit res ulla de se dicere, sum quod sum, cum & aliter sit, quam est. Est enim homo, praeter quod sit homo, etiam albus. Esse autem album, aliud est quam esse hominem. Sed esse justum Deo non est aliud quam esse Deum, esse bonum, esse sapientem, de sententia Bernhardi ad Eugenium & Augustini, nempe secundum naturam Dei.
english: Which is variously established. 1. God is not in a genus, but exceeds all things. But Being prescinds every generic mode of existing and leaves the significate in its infinite amplitude. For Being cannot be limited, but this and that being can. Being surpasses times, places, and modes of existing in them.

2. This vocabulary makes our mind wander to the infinite sea of the divine essence, so that we do not find where to stay the intuition. But he who thinks he finds something beyond Being has not yet had the ratio of being. 3. Being says the present of eternity, taking away future and past. For those are not in God, but in things that suffer succession. But succession is from mutability. Therefore it also indicates eternity and immutability. But no creature can be exquisitely named by this name insofar as it is a noun, but insofar as it is a participle. For they participate some entity, yet are not beings, but some beings. So man is not being, but some being. And although Being is predicated of all without addition, yet it is always understood with addition and contraction, but of God absolutely. And this is the difference between predicable being and first being, as in Thomas Aquinas in the little book On Being and Essence. For God is all things eminently. Therefore His name is every name, as Trismegistus said.

4. In every thing accident is found except in God. But accident differs from the substance of a thing. Therefore no thing can say of itself, I am what I am, since it also is otherwise than it is. For a man, besides being a man, is also white. But to be white is other than to be a man. But for God to be just is not other than to be God, to be good, to be wise — according to the judgment of Bernard to Eugenius and of Augustine, namely according to the nature of God.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): Which variously is established. 1. God is not in a genus, but all things exceeds. But Being every generic mode belonging toward existing prescinds plus ye significate in its infinite amplitude leaves. For Being cannot be limited, but this plus that being can. Being times, places, plus modes belonging toward existing in them surpasses. 2. This vocabulary makes our mind unto ye infinite sea belonging toward ye divine essence wander, so that where to stay ye intuition we do not find. But he who thinks something beyond Being he finds has not yet ye ratio belonging toward being had. 3. Being ye present belonging toward eternity says, future plus past taking away. For those are not in God, but in things that succession suffer. But succession from mutability is. Therefore also eternity plus immutability it indicates. But no creature by this name exquisitely can be named insofar as it is a noun, but insofar as a participle. For some entity they participate, yet are not beings, but some beings. So man is not being, but some being. And although Being of all without addition is predicated, yet always with addition plus contraction it is understood, but of God absolutely. And this stands as ye difference between predicable being plus first being, as in Thomas Aquinas in ye little book On Being plus Essence. For God all things eminently is. Therefore His name is every name, as Trismegistus said. 4. In every thing accident is found except in God. But accident from ye substance belonging toward a thing differs. Therefore no thing of itself can say, I am what I am, since also otherwise than it is it is. For a man, besides being a man, also white is. But to be white other than to be a man is. But for God to be just other than to be God, to be good, to be wise is not — according to ye judgment belonging toward Bernard unto Eugenius plus belonging toward Augustine, namely according to ye nature belonging toward God.

title: Formal rationes one in God; analogical ens; concrete names without composition
latin: Caeteroquin ista vocabula a nobis sumpta & inventa sunt, non ad significandum unum idemque, sed multas rationes formales. Dicitur enim ens quod habet essentiam. Sapiens cui res sapiunt, prout sunt. Bonus, qui est amabilis, ex hoc quod juvat alios. Omnes tamen istae rationes sunt una in Deo. Non enim alio est bonus, alio ens, alio justus, sed seipso est illa omnia: imo est qui est, non quae est, ut ait Bernhardus. Non enim ista sunt in eo divisa, etsi sint talia in nobis. Neque tamen, cum ista de Deo distincte enunciamus, nugamur, sed ut supra dictum est, dicimus multas rationes formales, quae tamen omnes, quamvis infinitae essent, exprimunt illud unum quod est Deus, fundans in sua infinitate omnes has rationes distinctas ratione &, ut sic loquar, idealiter, non in fundamento, sed in termino ratiocinii & in exemplari rerum nostrarum. Diximus ens de Deo & creaturis dici analogice. Deus igitur est ens per se, caetera entia non sunt nisi respectu ipsius, sicuti urina non est sana, nisi respectu sanitatis animalis, cujus est effectus & signum. Est igitur maxime proprium Dei, esse id quod est. Neque vox Deus ei est essentialius nomen, quam ens, nisi quantum ad nos, qui infinitatem entis non capientes ex aliquo effectu particulari Deum nominamus. Valet enim hic regula: Nomina concreta, cum de Deo dicuntur, non compositionem vel concretionem aliquam arguunt, sed ostendunt, ipsum esse rem per se subsistentem, seu suppositum.
english: Moreover these vocabularies have been taken and invented by us not for signifying one and the same thing, but many formal rationes. For being is said of what has essence; wise, of him to whom things taste as they are; good, of him who is lovable from this, that he helps others. Yet all these rationes are one in God. For He is not good by one thing, being by another, just by another, but by Himself is all those: indeed He is who is, not what is, as Bernard says. For these are not divided in Him, even if they are such in us. Nor yet, when we enunciate these distinctly of God, do we trifle, but as said above, we say many formal rationes which yet all, though they were infinite, express that one which is God, founding in His infinity all these rationes distinct by reason and, so to speak, ideally — not in the foundation, but in the term of the reasoning and in the exemplar of our things.

We said Being is said of God and creatures analogically. God therefore is being through Himself; the other beings are not except with respect to Him, just as urine is not healthy except with respect to the health of the animal, of which it is an effect and sign. It is therefore most proper to God to be that which is. Nor is the word God a more essential name for Him than Being, except as regards us, who not grasping the infinity of Being name God from some particular effect.
For here this rule holds: Concrete names, when they are said of God, do not argue any composition or concretion, but show that He Himself is a thing subsisting through Himself, or a suppositum.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): Moreover these vocabularies by us have been taken plus invented not for signifying one plus ye same thing, but many formal rationes. For being is said of what essence has; wise, of him unto whom things as they are taste; good, of him who lovable is from this, that others he helps. Yet all these rationes in God are one. For He is not good by one thing, being by another, just by another, but by Himself all those is: indeed He is who is, not what is, as Bernard says. For these in Him are not divided, even if in us such they are. Nor yet, when these distinctly of God we enunciate, do we trifle, but as above said, many formal rationes we say which yet all, though infinite they were, that one which is God express, founding in His infinity all these rationes distinct by reason plus, so to speak, ideally — not in ye foundation, but in ye term belonging toward ye reasoning plus in ye exemplar belonging toward our things. We said Being of God plus creatures analogically is said. God therefore is being through Himself; ye other beings are not except with respect unto Him, just as urine healthy is not except with respect unto ye health belonging toward ye animal, of which an effect plus sign it is. It is therefore most proper unto God to be that which is. Nor is ye word God a more essential name for Him than Being, except as regards us, who ye infinity belonging toward Being not grasping God from some particular effect name. For here this rule holds: Concrete names, when of God they are said, any composition or concretion do not argue, but show that He Himself a thing through Himself subsisting, or a suppositum, is.

title: Summum; vivens; integrity; independens; nature as Deity — Cap. 5 close of I
latin: Quoniam vero ens dividitur in substantiam & accidens: Deus ita ens est, ut quam maxime sit substantia, quia maxime per se subsistít & a nullo prorsus dependet, sed a semetipso, in semetipso, & per nihil aliud, quam per semetipsum est, quicquid est. Omne vero accidens supponit aliud ens, a quo sustentetur: at Deus, cum a seipso exsistat, necessario est primum ens, ideoque ab alio ente priori sustentari non potest. DEINDE, Deus hic dicitur ens summum, hoc est, perfectione cetera omnia post se relinquens, utpote, quorum est causa. Omnis enim causa princeps, de qua hic agimus, si producat effectum diversae a se rationis (quod hic necessario fieri debet) isto effectu est nobilior; id quod in Metaphysicis demonstratur. Atque hinc est, quod Dionysius dixit, res Deo esse similes, non autem Deum rebus, quoniam superexcedit, & a Deo habent, ut illum imitentur, non contra, ut patet ex Esai. 40.17.18; Rom. 1.23. TERTIO, cum duo sint potissimum, quibus essentialis substantiarum perfectio continetur, essentia nimirum ac vita, illa omnium, haec nonnullarum, ultra quae in iis mens humana nihil comprehendere potest: idcirco, ut essentia, ita & vita Deo meritissimo tribuitur, qua videlicet actuosus est in se & extra se; & sine qua caeterarum rerum causa esse nequit, ut inferius demonstrabitur. Hacpropter Deus in scripturis ens & vivens passim dicitur, Apocal. 1.8 & 4.8; Deut.; Psal. 18.47; 84.3; Jerem. 10.10; Ezech. 33.11; Dan. 4.34; Matth. 16.16; Joh. 5.26 & 6.57; Act. 14.15; Rom. 9.26. QUARTO, cum Deo, ut enti primo ac summo, vita conveniat modo perfectissimo, ideoque spiritualis, integritatem in ea merito consideramus, quae virtute ac beatitate continetur, Psal. 25; 1 Tim. 6.15. POSTREMO, additur in descriptione vox independens, quae hic est loco differentiae, Deumque a rebus creatis discriminat & significat tam essentiam quam vitam ita esse in Deo, ut is utramque habeat non aliunde, sed a seipso, Exod. 3.14; Psal. 36.10. E quibus omnibus firmiter colligitur, naturam Deo recte tribui, voce ista in laxiore significatu accepta, ut idem notet, quod ipsa Deitas, Col. 2.9. nimirum id, per quod Deus est Deus & ab omnibus aliis rebus differt. Hinc Paulus Gal. 4.8. Ignorantes Deum, ait, serviebatis iis, qui natura non sunt dii: indicans, eum solum esse verum Deum, qui est Deus natura, hoc est, qui essentiam & personas vere divinas habet.
english: But since being is divided into substance and accident: God is so being that He is substance as much as possible, because He most of all subsists through Himself and depends on nothing at all, but from Himself, in Himself, and through nothing other than through Himself is whatever He is. But every accident presupposes another being by which it is sustained: yet God, since He exists from Himself, is necessarily the first being, and therefore cannot be sustained by another prior being.

NEXT, God is here called the highest being, that is, leaving all the rest behind Himself in perfection, as being their cause. For every principal cause of which we treat here, if it produce an effect of a diverse ratio from itself (which here must necessarily happen), is nobler than that effect; which is demonstrated in the Metaphysics. And hence it is that Dionysius said things are like God, but not God like things, since He exceeds above, and they have from God that they imitate Him, not the reverse (Isaiah 40:17-18; Romans 1:23).

THIRD, since two things chiefly contain the essential perfection of substances, namely essence and life — that of all, this of some, beyond which the human mind can comprehend nothing in them — therefore, as essence, so also life is most deservedly attributed to God, by which namely He is active in Himself and outside Himself; and without which He cannot be the cause of the other things, as will be demonstrated below. For this reason God in the Scriptures is everywhere called being and living (Revelation 1:8 and 4:8; Deuteronomy; Psalm 18:47; 84:3; Jeremiah 10:10; Ezekiel 33:11; Daniel 4:34; Matthew 16:16; John 5:26 and 6:57; Acts 14:15; Romans 9:26). FOURTH, since life belongs to God as first and highest being in the most perfect manner, and therefore spiritual, we deservedly consider integrity in it, which is contained in virtue and beatitude (Psalm 25; 1 Timothy 6:15). LASTLY, the word independent is added in the description, which here stands in place of a difference, and discriminates God from created things, and signifies that both essence and life are so in God that He has each not from elsewhere but from Himself (Exodus 3:14; Psalm 36:10). From all which it is firmly gathered that nature is rightly attributed to God, that word taken in a looser significate, so that it notes the same as Deity itself (Colossians 2:9) — namely that through which God is God and differs from all other things. Hence Paul (Galatians 4:8): Not knowing God, he says, you served those who by nature are not gods — indicating that He alone is the true God who is God by nature, that is, who has a truly divine essence and persons.
pass_a: Pass A clause gloss (reordered): But since being into substance plus accident is divided: God so being is that substance as much as possible He is, because most of all through Himself He subsists plus on nothing at all depends, but from Himself, in Himself, plus through nothing other than through Himself is whatever He is. But every accident another being by which it is sustained presupposes: yet God, since from Himself He exists, necessarily ye first being is, plus therefore by another prior being cannot be sustained. NEXT, God here ye highest being is called, that is, all ye rest behind Himself in perfection leaving, as being their cause. For every principal cause of which here we treat, if an effect of a diverse ratio from itself it produce (which here necessarily must happen), nobler than that effect is; which in ye Metaphysics is demonstrated. And hence it is that Dionysius said things unto God are like, but not God unto things, since above He exceeds, plus from God they have that Him they imitate, not ye reverse (Isaiah 40:17-18; Romans 1:23). THIRD, since two things chiefly ye essential perfection belonging toward substances contain, namely essence plus life — that of all, this of some, beyond which ye human mind nothing in them can comprehend — therefore, as essence, so also life most deservedly unto God is attributed, by which namely in Himself plus outside Himself He is active; plus without which ye cause belonging toward ye other things He cannot be, as below will be demonstrated. For this reason God in ye Scriptures everywhere being plus living is called (Revelation 1:8 plus 4:8; Deuteronomy; Psalm 18:47; 84:3; Jeremiah 10:10; Ezekiel 33:11; Daniel 4:34; Matthew 16:16; John 5:26 plus 6:57; Acts 14:15; Romans 9:26). FOURTH, since life unto God as first plus highest being in ye most perfect manner belongs, plus therefore spiritual, integrity in it we deservedly consider, which in virtue plus beatitude is contained (Psalm 25; 1 Timothy 6:15). LASTLY, ye word independent in ye description is added, which here in place belonging toward a difference stands, plus God from created things discriminates, plus signifies that both essence plus life so in God are that each not from elsewhere but from Himself He has (Exodus 3:14; Psalm 36:10). From all which firmly it is gathered that nature unto God rightly is attributed, that word in a looser significate taken, so that ye same as Deity itself it notes (Colossians 2:9) — namely that through which God is God plus from all other things differs. Hence Paul (Galatians 4:8): Not knowing God, he says, those who by nature are not gods you served — indicating that He alone ye true God is who God by nature is, that is, who a truly divine essence plus persons has.

title: II. God's nature viewed in essence and persons — Cap. 5 close
latin: II. Natura Dei spectatur in essentia & personis. Cognitio unius essentiae petitur e libro naturae & scripturae conjunctim: cognitio trium distinctarum personarum ex libro scripturae tantum. Essentiae nomen vere Deo convenire, ex hoc intelligimus, quod is est ens primum & summum, a quo caetera entia omnia dependent. Si vero ens est, utique habet essentiam: cum per eam ens necessario definiatur. Et, quia Deus essentiam a seipso habet, & non aliunde; ideoque eam perpetuo possidet; in abstracto quoque essentia esse dicitur: unde Hieronymus tom. 2. epistola ad Damasum: Una, inquit, Dei & sola natura, quae vere est. Id enim, quod subsistít, non habet aliunde, sed suum est. Caetera, quae creata sunt, etiamsi videntur esse, non sunt, quia aliquando non fuerunt, & possunt rursum non esse quod fuerunt. Deus solus, qui aeternus est, hoc est, qui exordium non habet, essentiae nomen vere tenet. De nomine personarum e scriptura 1 Joh. 5.7; Heb. 1.3. interius videbitur.
english: II. The nature of God is viewed in essence and persons. Knowledge of the one essence is sought from the book of nature and of Scripture jointly: knowledge of the three distinct persons from the book of Scripture alone.

That the name of essence truly belongs to God we understand from this, that He is the first and highest being, on whom all other beings depend. But if He is being, He certainly has essence: since by it being is necessarily defined. And because God has essence from Himself and not from elsewhere, and therefore possesses it perpetually, He is also said to be essence in the abstract: from which Jerome (tome 2, letter to Damasus): One, he says, and only nature of God, which truly is. For that which subsists does not have from elsewhere, but is its own. The rest which are created, even if they seem to be, are not, because once they were not, and can again not be what they were. God alone, who is eternal — that is, who has no beginning — truly holds the name of essence.
Concerning the name of the persons from Scripture (1 John 5:7; Hebrews 1:3) it will be seen more inwardly.
